items.title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
items.raw_text: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. items.title: Futures Club #6: You Can’t Create What You Can’t Imagine
items.raw_text: How can libraries help people think about the future? One of the clearest lessons from Futures Club #6, with Thomas Sture Rasmussen and Lotte Hviid Dhyrbye from the Danish Library Association was was that the answer is not to predict what will happen. Instead, libraries can give people the tools, spaces and confidence to explore different possible futures for themselves. The Association’s work was built on a combination of practical experience, as well as the record of the Library of the Future think-tank. The think tank had started as a form of aggregator, bringing together data and thinkers to prepare reports setting out visions of the future of libraries. However, over time, the emphasis shifted towards how to equip libraries to ask their own questions and imagine their own possibilities. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) had been particularly useful in this process. They provide both inspiration and a framework for conversations about the future we want. This can help overcome apathy, but also polarisation: instead of beginning with entrenched positions, people can start by discussing possibilities and shared aspirations. The SDGs have also helped libraries open conversations with organisations and sectors beyond the library field. items.title: A chance for a comprehensive approach? Knowledge and information in the 2026 Voluntary National Reviews
items.raw_text: Governments are recognising the role of knowledge and information in achieving progress across the United Nations’ 2030 Agenda, both as goals in themselves and as an enabler. They also underline the need for specialists, infrastructures, and intermediation. Yet a scattered way of doing things risks missing out on opportunities for a more strategic appraoch, notably one that realises the potential of libraries. IFLA has released its analysis of the 2026 Voluntary National Reviews (VNRs) of implementation of the SDGs, from the perspective of the contribution made by knowledge and information. The wealth of references to this serve as a strong indicator of both the strength and richness of this role. While there is unevenness in the number and variety of references from one Review to the next, these are present in every single review. As a result, both individually and collectively, the data points to a strong recognition of the different dimensions of the role of knowledge and information in sustainable development – as goals in their own right, and as an enabler of other goals. Some countries do look to measure these, but only in relatively narrow ways. There is also evidence of reflection on the need to uphold information integrity becoming part of wider sustainable development agendas. Working in the Department of Foreign Relations at Türkiye’s Directorate General for Libraries and Publications, international cooperation was already part of my professional life. WLIC allowed me to experience the people behind that work. Being among more than 3,000 participants from over 100 countries and regions showed me that international librarianship depends as much on listening and understanding as on exchanging knowledge. For me, this connected closely to cultural diplomacy: cooperation often begins by understanding how others work, what they value and the challenges they face. As a Discovery Grant recipient, I attended business meetings on public libraries, national libraries, library design and literacy. I was interested in seeing how IFLA works from within: how priorities are discussed, different views are considered and members turn experience into collective work. items.raw_text: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! items.title: What happened at COP31, and what does it mean for the library field?
items.raw_text: In short: Despite COP31 ending without key cover agreements, actors from the culture sector made strong cases for our role in climate empowerment, adaptation, and resilience. Parties were unable to come to an agreement on the next Action for Climate Empowerment (ACE) action plan, although drafts had promising inclusion of information integrity and culture sector actors. IFLA’s volunteers, members, and partners had a record-breaking year for showcasing libraries of all kinds as drivers of climate action. Libraries showed real leadership in the culture sector, including through securing endorsements of heritage-based climate adaptation, the first Climate Library at a COP, and library commitments in the Heritage Adapts! initiative. We need community actors for climate now more than ever At the UN Climate Change Conference (COP), decisions require a compromise between national governments – including on a cover agreement. This is the conference’s key declaration of commitments countries will take on climate change. Consensus was not reaches due to the removal of fossil fuels from the draft declaration, which some States felt was unacceptable. While other decisions were made, the inability to agree on a core political outcome is widely considered a disappointment. Now more than ever, the role of communities, cities and local governments, civil society groups and institutions like libraries is needed to help people feel connected and empowered to make positive change. items.title: Management consulting is not a thin wrapper on intelligence
items.raw_text: By Rod Moshtagi and Sayash Kapoor. Moshtagi is a researcher at the Harvard Kennedy School and was previously a senior associate at PwC. In summer 2026, he was a GovAI fellow advised by Kapoor, and the research for this essay began as part of the fellowship. Many discussions of AI’s economic impact rest on the implicit assumption that most knowledge work is a “thin wrapper” on intelligence. In this view, the main job of a knowledge worker is to process information. Once AI can match the quality of expert responses in a domain, it should be able to take over most of the work in that domain. Management consulting is a compelling example. The visible outputs of consultants, such as research summaries, slide decks, and financial models, primarily comprise processing information , work that AI already excels at. If the main function of a consulting firm is to provide information, AI looks like an existential threat. Many commentators have drawn this conclusion. items.raw_text: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well. Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm. This thinking isn’t all that fringe. items.raw_text: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. items.raw_text: On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug. The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise. The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week. items.raw_text: Big Tech hangt zware strafmaatregelen boven het hoofd als buiten de VS datacenters worden gebouwd. Donald Trump dreigt met ‘enorme sancties’ als dit blijft doorgaan. ‘We staan niet toe dat datacenters naar andere landen verhuizen, want China zal ze allemaal in handen krijgen, en dat laten we niet gebeuren. Het dreigement van Trump komt in een periode dat Amerikanen zich meer verzetten tegen de bouw van ai-datacenters in hun nabijheid. Trump vindt echter dat Amerikanen deze projecten juist moeten omarmen. Hij moedigde lokale gemeenschappen aan om concessies af te dwingen van ontwikkelaars. Mogelijke aanleiding voor de dreiging met sancties is dat Canada zich steeds meer profileert als een hub voor hyperscalers.
